beats.narration: Your build runs. The most expensive thing on a team is the engineering time spent rebuilding that same thing for the next customer. The fix is the accelerator: a solution packaged so the next engagement starts from a working foundation instead of a blank repository. Take the working build, separate what's customer-specific, and expose those values as parameters with documented defaults. Configure — don't rewrite.

elements.text: the priciest line item: rebuilding the same thing

beats.narration: Reusable work comes in three shapes, and each packages differently. The agent template bundles the system prompt, tool schemas, and loop structure — packaging means pulling the domain values into configuration, so a new team sets values instead of editing the loop. The MCP server package bundles the tools and their scopes — packaging means documenting every input and letting the installing team set the scope, so it installs with zero code edits. And the eval suite bundles the graded set and judge rubric, shipped together so a new team proves the asset still works in their context. That same suite doubles as the deployment gate later. The classic wrong shape is a pile of loose scripts. They run, so they look reusable — but every value hides in a different file, and the next team copies and diverges.

items.text: MCP server — documented inputs, installer sets scope
eval suite — dataset + rubric travel together

elements.text:
✗ loose scripts: they RUN, so they LOOK reusable —
then every team copies and diverges

beats.narration: Two more things go in the box. Documentation covers what nobody can infer from the source: the environment assumptions, the expected inputs, the failure modes already handled, and the eval that defines working. Without it, the next team treats the asset as a black box and rebuilds it anyway. And the audit bundle: what data the asset touches, what identity it acts under, what log it leaves. An accelerator without those passes the demo and stalls at the first security review.

elements.text: also in the box: docs + audit

items.text: docs = what source can't say: assumptions · inputs · handled failures
audit = data touched · identity used · log left

elements.text:
no audit bundle → passes the demo,
stalls at the security review

beats.narration: The watch-out is a postmortem. A team hardcoded the demo values to hit a deadline — the repo path, the model name, the thresholds, some prompt fragments — shipped on time, and labeled the build reusable. Months later a second team picked it up and found nothing to configure: every changing value was baked into the loop, no document said which values were customer-specific, and there was no bundled eval to confirm anything after they guessed at edits. They rewrote it from scratch. The trap is that a working template doesn't announce that it can't be reused. The cost appears only when the second team pays it.

elements.text: watch out: shipped fast, reused never

items.text: no parameters — values baked into the loop
no bundled eval to confirm the guesses

elements.text:
a working template never announces
it can't be reused
the cost lands on the NEXT team

beats.narration: The reflex: package while the build is fresh, because the knowledge of what's customer-specific is the most expensive thing to reconstruct later. One honest exception — a true one-off nobody will reuse: skip the overhead and just ship. Next, the checkpoint hands you a broken template. Then: contributing back.
